    The part that nobody mentions is that the tool was written for a team of four and is now carrying a team of two hundred, which is a different problem wearing the same name and answering to the same command line, with the same four defaults.

    We kept it because rewriting it would have cost a quarter, and every quarter since then somebody has proposed the rewrite, priced it at a quarter, and been told that this is not the quarter for it. I have seen that meeting four times.

  2. bob 1 hour ago | link | reply

    My experience was the opposite: the small team wrote something general enough that the large team never had to think about it, and the only reason anyone remembers it exists is the one morning a year when the certificate expires and the whole building learns the name of a program written before most of them were hired. The rest of the year it runs without a single ticket, which in my book is the best thing you can say about any tool at all.
